Students now see how his grief, confusion and longing for a safe place are shown through dreams, the Minotaur horn and the camp setting.","enduringUnderstanding":"Authors use word choice, tone and details to show what characters fear and hope for, and different versions of a story (print and film) create different experiences of the same event.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 13 (Chapter 7) students will cite details about the cabins, tables and traditions of Camp Half-Blood to see how Percy's new life is organized. Tracking Percy's feelings of belonging here prepares them for that work.","performanceTask":"Shared Stories, Shared Lessons: tracing how a theme develops across part of a narrative, and comparing versions of a story, build the cross-text comparison and adaptation analysis the culminating writing requires."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"pinochle","definition":"a card game played by two to four players (p. 57)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"hovered","definition":"stayed in the air near one place, or waited close by (p. 57)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"smirking","definition":"smiling in an unpleasant, self-satisfied way (p. 57)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"scorpion","definition":"a small, venomous creature with pincers and a curved stinging tail (p. 58)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"satyr","definition":"in Greek myth, a creature that is half man and half goat (p. 59)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"minotaurs","definition":"in Greek myth, monsters with a human body and a bull's head (p. 59)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"pavilion","definition":"a large open building or covered area used for gatherings (p. 62)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mischievous","definition":"playfully causing trouble (p. 63)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"gladiator","definition":"in ancient Rome, a person trained to fight in public shows (p. 65)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"typical","definition":"having the usual qualities of a certain type; normal (p. 66)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"tone","definition":"the attitude a writer or narrator shows toward a subject","tier":"support"},{"word":"mood","definition":"the feeling a reader gets from a text","tier":"support"},{"word":"disoriented","definition":"confused about where you are or what is happening","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 57–66"},{"title":"Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief (2010 film), Minotaur scene","author":"Directed by Chris Columbus","pages":"Minotaur scene clip"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate their thinking about how it feels to be in a new place and begin thinking about Percy's fears and hopes about belonging.","activities":[{"id":"launch-new-place-turn-and-talk","title":"Turn and Talk: Arriving Somewhere New","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.2"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with a partner. Think of a time you arrived somewhere new, such as a new school, a new team, or a new neighborhood. What did you hope for, and what did you fear?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What makes a place feel like somewhere you belong, and what makes it feel strange?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When I started at my new school I hoped someone would sit with me at lunch, but I was afraid nobody would. A place feels like I belong when people know my name. It feels strange when I don't know the rules."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Percy ends Chapter 4 in a place that is completely new, and he is grieving his mother. Today you'll read to find out what he fears and what he hopes for as he tries to belong. You'll also compare how the book and the movie show the same scene."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Some students may have moved or lost someone close to them. Invite sharing without requiring personal detail; students may talk about a book or movie character instead."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students learn Chapter 5 vocabulary in context, study consonant digraphs, and see how complex sentences signal comparison and contrast.","activities":[{"id":"lab-vocabulary-in-context","title":"Vocabulary in Context and Digraph Study","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Introduce New Words","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 57–66"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's learn some of today's words from the pages themselves. Turn to page 57. Find *pinochle*, *hovered*, and *smirking*. Read the sentences around each word. *Hovered* shows someone staying close by, waiting. *Smirking* is not a friendly smile. Notice that the authors' word choices give the scene a tense feel before anything happens."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at *smirking* on page 57. What does this word tell you about the character that *smiling* would not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"*Smirking* tells me the character is enjoying something unkind or knows something Percy doesn't. *Smiling* would sound friendly, but *smirking* makes me feel uneasy."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Now look at the sounds. Say *scorpion* (p. 58), *mischievous* (p. 63) and *typical* (p. 66). Find the consonant digraphs: two letters that make one sound. In *mischievous* the *ch* makes a *ch* sound, as in *chief*, and in *scorpion* the *c* is a hard /k/ sound followed by *p*. Say *satyr* and *pavilion* and clap the syllables. Digraphs like *ch*, *sh*, *th*, *wh*, *ph* and *ck* help us decode longer words one chunk at a time."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which digraphs can you find in *mischievous* and *typical*, and what sounds do they make?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In *mischievous* there is *sch*, with *ch* making a /ch/ sound, and in *typical* there isn't a digraph, but the *c* is a hard /k/ sound. I can break *mis-chie-vous* into three parts to read it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Several words are myth terms (*satyr*, *minotaurs*, *gladiator*, *pavilion*) that students will meet again. Show a quick picture if available. Save *scorpion*, *gladiator*, *mischievous* and *typical* for the reading to see them in context. Be accurate: not every target word contains a digraph, so focus on the ones that do and on chunking."}]},{"id":"lab-comparison-sentences","title":"Complex Sentences for Comparison and Contrast","minutes":5,"standards":["L.6.6","RL.6.7"],"routine":"Sentence Combining","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Today you'll compare the book to the film. Words like *although*, *whereas*, *while* and *however* show contrast. Watch me combine two simple sentences. *The book describes Percy's thoughts. The film shows his face.* Combined: *While the book describes Percy's thoughts, the film shows his face.* I can also write: *The book describes Percy's thoughts; however, the film shows his face.*"},{"type":"directions","text":"Combine each pair into one sentence that shows a contrast. Use although, whereas, while, or however.\n1. The narrator uses a calm tone. The scene is terrifying.\n2. In the book, Percy hears the horn in his mind. In the film, the audience hears it through music and sound effects."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which word did you choose, and what relationship does it show?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I wrote, *Although the narrator uses a calm tone, the scene is terrifying.* *Although* shows two things that seem like opposites. For number 2 I wrote, *In the book Percy hears the horn in his mind, whereas in the film the audience hears it through sound effects.*"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Remind students that a sentence beginning with *Although* or *While* needs a comma after the first part, and that *however* after a semicolon is followed by a comma."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students closely read pp. 57–66 to analyze word choice, mood, and the emergence of grief, identity and belonging. Part B: Students compare the book's Minotaur incident with the 2010 film using a two-column organizer.","activities":[{"id":"lia-close-read-word-choice","title":"Part A: Close Read for Word Choice and Theme","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.1","RL.6.2","L.6.5.a"],"routine":"Close Read & Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 57–66"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 57–66. Annotate three kinds of details: (1) vivid phrases about Percy's world after his mother's disappearance, (2) phrases that show his dreams and his reaction to the Minotaur horn, and (3) phrases that describe Camp Half-Blood and his disorientation there. Record each phrase in a chart with two columns: *Phrase from the text* and *Mood or tone it creates*."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Word choice means the exact words an author picks. *Connotation* is the feeling attached to a word. Notice *hovered* and *smirking* on p. 57: both words carry a sense of threat, so the mood is uneasy. Compare the words used for the camp on p. 62 with those for Percy's dreams. Look for where Percy feels afraid and where he feels hope."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Choose one vivid phrase about Percy's world after his mother's disappearance. What mood does it create?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The words about the empty, quiet world after his mom is gone make the mood sad and lonely. The word choice shows that Percy is grieving and doesn't know where he fits anymore."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Percy react to the Minotaur horn, and what does that reaction show about his fears?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy reacts with alarm and confusion, which shows his fear that the danger from before has followed him. The reaction shows he doesn't feel safe yet, even at a place meant to protect him."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the description of Camp Half-Blood suggest about Percy's hopes about belonging, and why does he feel disoriented?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The camp has strange things like a satyr and a pavilion, so Percy is disoriented, but the details also show a community with a place for people like him. He hopes he can belong, but he is afraid he won't understand the rules. Grief, identity and belonging start to show up together."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and evaluating the author's language choices to explain mood and theme.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to one word that makes the scene feel tense or sad. Then use a frame. Frames: The word ___ creates a ___ mood because ___. Percy feels ___ because the text says ___. This detail shows that Percy is afraid of ___ but hopes for ___. Remind students to use simple present tense to discuss the text (Percy feels, the author uses) and past tense to retell events (Percy heard the horn).","watchFor:":"","watchFor":"If students name only a feeling and give no phrase → Prompt: \"Which exact words show that feeling?\" If students retell the plot instead of analyzing → Prompt: \"What mood do those words create?\" Success: Student quotes a phrase and explains its mood or connotation using a frame and the correct verb tense."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4"],"stem":"On p. 57, the narrator describes a character as *smirking* and *hovering*. How does this word choice affect the mood of the scene?","choices":[{"text":"It makes the scene feel tense and threatening because the words suggest unkind or watchful behavior.","correct":true,"rationale":"Both words carry negative connotations that create an uneasy mood."},{"text":"It makes the scene feel funny and relaxed because the character is smiling.","correct":false,"rationale":"This ignores that *smirking* is an unkind smile, not a friendly one."},{"type":"x","text":"It shows the character is helping Percy feel safe.","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may misread the character's motives; the word choices suggest threat, not comfort."},{"text":"It has no effect because it only tells where characters are standing.","correct":false,"rationale":"Students may treat the words as plain description, but word choice shapes mood."}]},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: identifying how word choice shapes mood","tryThis":"Give students a feelings word bank (uneasy, lonely, hopeful, confused) and have them match each to one quoted phrase before explaining. Provide the frame: The word ___ makes me feel ___ because ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find a phrase on pp. 57–66 with a different connotation from the others and explain how it shifts the mood from fear to hope, using one complex sentence with *although* or *while*."}]}]},{"id":"lia-book-vs-film","title":"Part B: Compare the Book and the 2010 Film","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.7","RL.6.4","RL.6.1","RL.6.6"],"routine":"Two-Column Graphic Organizer","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 57–66"},{"type":"directions","text":"Draw a two-column organizer. Label the left column *Book* and the right column *2010 Film*. In each column take notes on (1) what happens in the Minotaur incident, (2) the emotions the main characters feel, and (3) the tone of the narrator or film. First, complete the left column from the book. Then watch the Minotaur scene in the 2010 film and complete the right column with the same questions. Below the organizer, write notes contrasting what you \"see\" and \"hear\" when reading with what you perceive when you watch."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In a book, the narrator's voice tells us what Percy thinks and how events feel, and we picture everything ourselves. In a film, we see faces, hear music and sound effects, and watch the director's choices. Watch and listen for the details that match the book and the details that are different."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Play only the Minotaur scene clip and replay once if time allows. Preview the clip; it contains fantasy action. Pause after the first viewing so students can fill in the right column. Students should compare the same incident, not retell the whole film."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one emotion Percy feels in the book, and how does the film show it differently?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In the book we read Percy's fear and confusion in the narrator's words. In the film we see it on his face and hear it in the music and sound effects, so we don't need the narrator to tell us."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How is the tone in the book different from the tone in the film?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Although the book's narrator sounds sarcastic and personal, the film feels more like an action movie with loud music. The book lets me hear Percy's voice, whereas the film focuses on what I see."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you see and hear in your mind when reading that you perceive differently when you watch?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When I read, I imagine what the Minotaur looks like and how the horn sounds, but in the film the director decides this for me. The film can make the scene faster and louder, while reading lets me slow down and think about Percy's feelings."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in viewing closely and evaluating how the language of print and the choices of film each present ideas.","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner one thing you read and one thing you saw. Frames: In the book, the narrator says ___, but in the film we see ___. The book makes me feel ___, whereas the film makes me feel ___. Although the film shows ___, the book explains ___. Model past tense for events (Percy ran) and present tense for analysis (the film shows).","watchFor":"If students describe only the film or only the book → Prompt: \"What is the same, and what is different?\" If students say one is simply better → Prompt: \"What does each version let you notice?\" Success: Student uses a contrast word and names a specific see/hear difference."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.7"],"stem":"Which statement best describes a difference between reading the Minotaur incident and watching it in the 2010 film?","choices":[{"text":"The film adds music, sound effects and visible faces, while the book relies on the narrator's words and the reader's imagination.","correct":true,"rationale":"This accurately contrasts what a reader pictures and hears with what a viewer perceives."},{"text":"The film and the book give exactly the same experience because the events are the same.","correct":false,"rationale":"Same events can feel different because the medium changes how they are presented."},{"text":"The book shows nothing about the characters' emotions, but the film shows all of them.","correct":false,"rationale":"The narrator describes the characters' emotions in detail."},{"text":"The film is longer, so it has more tone than the book.","correct":false,"rationale":"Tone is about attitude and word choice, not length."}]},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: comparing the book and film","tryThis":"Give a pre-labeled organizer with the rows Events, Feelings, Tone, See, Hear. Pause the clip after each key moment so students can write a few words. Provide the frame: In the book ___, but in the film ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain which version better shows Percy's fears about belonging and why, and to write one sentence using *whereas* and one using *however* to support their view."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students answer the text-dependent question and reflect on how word choice and format shape understanding.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflection","title":"Reflection: Percy's Fears and Hopes","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.7","RL.6.2"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Connect to the Performance Task: in *Shared Stories, Shared Lessons* students will compare versions of a story and trace how a theme develops. Today's work with theme, word choice and the film comparison practices both skills."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the paragraph:\n\nIn Chapter 5, the author shows Percy's fear of ___ and his hope for ___. The phrase \"___\" creates a ___ mood. Although the book ___, the film ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 5, the author shows Percy's fear of being alone and not understanding the world of the camp, and his hope of finding a place where he belongs. The phrase about the horn creates an alarming mood. Although the book lets me hear Percy's thoughts, the film shows his fear through his face and the music."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Students continue reading to follow Percy's experiences at camp.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch5-7","title":"Read and Annotate","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Independent Reading","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read the summary of Chapter 5 (pp. 67–74), Chapter 6 (full), and Chapter 7 (pp. 93 through the top of p. 100, ending \"...as if drawing a battle plan.\"). Then read and annotate Chapter 7 from p. 100 (\"Back at cabin eleven,...\") to p. 106. Mark one detail that shows Percy feeling like he does or does not belong."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students closely read Chapter 5 (pp. 57–66) to analyze how word choice creates mood and how grief, identity and belonging begin to emerge in Percy's dreams, his reaction to the Minotaur horn, and the camp description.
